title: Juan Atkins, Detroit Techno Architect Behind Model 500's "No UFO's," Dies at 64

content:
Juan Atkins, the Detroit visionary who dreamed up a new sound from synthesizers, funk and science fiction and then gave it the name the whole world now uses, techno, died October 31 in Mexico City. He was 64. He had travelled there to share his music with fans at YuYu Cine Club over the Día de los Muertos weekend, still doing what he loved more than four decades after he helped invent an entire genre.

Tributes have poured in from across the music world. “Juan was the originator of Techno, a true visionary who opened the door for so many of us, myself included,” wrote his lifelong friend Kevin Saunderson. Fatboy Slim called him a true pioneer, and Detroit Mayor Mary Sheffield honoured his contributions to the city that shaped him and that he, in turn, helped put on the global musical map.

Juan Atkins was born September 12, 1962, in Detroit, where his father worked as a concert promoter. Music surrounded him from the start, and as a boy he played guitar and bass in funk and garage bands with his friends. When his family moved to nearby Belleville, Michigan, he met two fellow students who would become his creative brothers, Derrick May and Kevin Saunderson. Together they would become known as the Belleville Three. At 15, Atkins bought his first synthesizer, a Korg MS-10, and his imagination took flight.

He drew inspiration from everywhere. George Clinton’s Parliament and Funkadelic sparked what he called his musical awakening, the late night radio shows of Detroit’s legendary DJ The Electrifying Mojo opened his ears to adventurous sounds, and the precise electronic pop of Kraftwerk showed him what machines could do. He was also fascinated by the futurist writing of sociologist Alvin Toffler, whose ideas about technology and society fed directly into Atkins’s vision of a music for the future.

In 1980 he formed Cybotron with Richard “3070” Davis. Their 1982 electro track “Clear” is often cited as the moment techno was born, and their 1983 debut album, ‘Enter,’ brought tracks like “Alleys of Your Mind,” “Cosmic Raindance” and “Techno City” into the world, music that married dystopian science fiction to irresistible grooves. After the duo went their separate ways in 1985, Atkins founded his own label, Metroplex, giving himself and other Detroit artists a home for their boldest ideas.

That same year he began recording as Model 500, and his debut single, “No UFO’s,” became a cornerstone of the genre, later named among the greatest dance songs of all time. “Night Drive,” “Testing 1-2,” “Play It Cool,” “Sound of Stereo,” “Interference,” “The Chase” and “Ocean to Ocean” followed, along with the Channel One singles “Technicolor” and “It’s Channel One” with Doug Craig. In 1988 his track “Techno Music” helped give the movement its name, and the sound he, May and Saunderson created soon crossed the Atlantic and ignited dance floors across Europe.

Atkins built deep ties with the European scene, particularly in Berlin. With Thomas Fehlmann and Moritz von Oswald he recorded as 3MB, releasing “Jazz Is the Teacher” and an album in 1992. As Model 500 he released ‘Classics’ in 1993, the albums ‘Deep Space’ in 1995 and ‘Mind and Body’ in 1999, and singles including “I See the Light,” “Sonic Sunset,” “The Flow,” “Starlight,” “I Wanna Be There” and “Be Brave.” Under his Infiniti alias he released ‘The Infiniti Collection’ in 1996 and the album ‘Skynet’ in 1998. ‘The Berlin Sessions’ arrived in 2005, and ‘20 Years 1985 to 2005’ celebrated two decades of Metroplex.

His creative spirit never slowed. Reuniting with Moritz von Oswald as Borderland, he released ‘Borderland’ in 2013 and ‘Transport’ in 2016, the latter celebrating 25 years of the famed Berlin label Tresor. As Model 500 he returned with ‘Digital Solutions’ in 2015, the same year he marked Metroplex’s 30th anniversary with a collaboration with VAVA Eyewear. In 2017 he recorded ‘Mind Merge’ with Orlando Voorn as Frequency vs Atkins, and joined May and Saunderson on a Belleville Three world tour. In 2019 he brought Cybotron to the stage for the very first time, launching the live show at London’s Barbican with dazzling visuals and fresh music. His story was celebrated in the documentaries ‘High Tech Soul,’ ‘Black to Techno’ and ‘God Said Give ’Em Drum Machines.’

AllMusic called him the godfather of techno and described his catalogue as perhaps the most influential body of work in the genre, while Mixmag hailed him as the original pioneer of Detroit techno. Yet for all the titles, those who knew him spoke most about his generosity, his work ethic and the way he guided younger artists. Generations of DJs and producers, from Detroit to Berlin to Tokyo, trace their musical roots directly back to his records.

From a teenager in Belleville experimenting with his first synthesizer to a global ambassador still bringing his music to new fans in Mexico City, Juan Atkins spent his life imagining the future and then building it. Every time a techno track pulses through a club anywhere in the world, the vision that began with three friends from Belleville plays on.
